title: Platform Decision Catalog: Degradation Strategies and Tradeoffs
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:

This decision catalog defines the pragmatic degradation strategies we use across the Redwood platform, explains when to apply each strategy, and captures tradeoffs (latency, cost, user experience, and operational complexity). It is a decision-first reference intended for oncall engineers, SREs designing SLIs/SLOs, and product/infra engineers implementing fallbacks.

Intended audience:
- SREs and platform engineers responsible for runtime behavior
- Product and infra owners evaluating user-impact tradeoffs
- Oncall responders using runbooks during partial outages

High-level principles (why this matters):
1) Prioritize correctness and safety over aggressive cost-saving when a request affects data integrity.
2) For user-facing latency SLOs, prefer graceful degradation (partial results, cached responses, reduced model size) over hard failures.
3) Make degradation observable: every fallback path must emit a clear telemetry tag, a metric, and a dashboard row.
4) Safe defaults first: automated policies must include low-risk, reversible actions (e.g., preforking, cache warmups) before irreversible ones (e.g., model downgrade that changes semantics).

Decision matrix (apply per service):
- Rows: Service criticality (P0-online, P1-core, P2-noncritical)
- Columns: Impact vector (latency-sensitive, correctness-sensitive, cost-driven)

Example decision outcomes:
- P0-online + latency-sensitive => keep fast model variants, enable KV prefix cache, partial token streaming, abort long-horizon requests with 95th pct cutoff.
- P1-core + correctness-sensitive => prefer queueing with bounded backlog, backpressure propagated to clients with Retry-After, disable model quantization rollouts during sustained errors.
- P2-noncritical + cost-driven => allow burst to shared-pool with soft-quotas, autoscale down aggressive batching, enable approximate reranks.

Tradeoffs table (text table):
Strategy | Visible UX | Cost | Latency | Operational complexity
-------- | ----------- | ---- | ------- | ----------------------
Prefix cache – fresh | Partial fast hits | medium | improves p50/p90 | low (cache ops)
Model downgrade | may change output | low | improves p99 | medium (monitor regressions)
Queueing/backpressure | increase tail | neutral | worsens p99 | medium (client contracts)
Partial response (early_stop) | degraded content | low | improves tail | low
Fallback model (smaller) | semantic variation | low | improves tail | high (eval/regrade)
Graceful shed (soft quota) | some clients slowed | saves cost | unpredictable | low

Implementation patterns and telemetry requirements:
1) Telemetry contract: every degraded path must emit: "degradation.type", "degradation.reason", "degradation.variant", and boolean "degradation.automated". These must be included in token-level traces and aggregated as counters and histograms.
2) Dashboards: for each service, add a "Degradation" row that shows: monthly count, current RPS of degraded requests, and recent regression alerts.
3) Alerting: define a tiered alert structure (see "Alert rules" below).

When to automate vs manual:
- Automate low-risk actions: cache warming, KV prefix reuse, soft-quota throttles with prioritized tenant buckets.
- Require human approval for model downgrades that cross quantization or architecture boundaries.
- Autoscaling policies can be automated under SLO-safe conditions (e.g., open CPU headroom and bounded queue length), otherwise require passive scaling and operator notification.

Standard runbook recipe (for oncall):
1) Triage: identify which degradation metric is spiking (degradation.count, kv_cache_hit_rate drop, queue_length).
2) Fast mitigation (2-10 min): enable temporary prefix-cache preload, toggle to warmed model variant, adjust soft-quota threshold to prioritize P0 tenants.
3) Stabilize (10-60 min): start graceful throttling for noncritical tenants, roll back any risky model downgrades, and open an incident if degradation persists.
4) Post-incident: capture decisions in a retrospective and add/update an entry in this decision catalog.

Example alert rules (text snippets):
- Critical: IF degradation.count / total_requests > 0.005 over 5m AND p99_latency degraded by > 30% THEN PAGER, runbook: "degradation-critical-handling"
- Warning: IF degradation.count increased by 3x week-over-week over 15m THEN slack-alert to platform-degradation-channel
- Regression: IF new_deployment AND degradation.count > baseline*1.5 over 30m THEN rollout-auto-hold and notify release-owner

Example safe throttle policy (YAML-like pseudocode):
throttle_policy: 
  name: soft-quota-slice-v1
  targets: ["noncritical-tenants"]
  priority_buckets:
    - name: p0
      weight: 100
    - name: p1
      weight: 50
    - name: p2
      weight: 10
  burst_window: 60s
  refill_rate: 200req/s
  eviction_policy: least_recent
  metrics: ["degradation.count","p99_latency","queue_length"]

Dashboard sample widgets (implementation notes):
- Degradation heatmap: service x region matrix showing normalized degradation_rate
- Time series: degradation.count (1m/5m/1h), p99 latency, kv_cache_hit_rate
- Per-tenant top 10 degraders with recent traffic trends

Rollout guidance (how to release new degradation automation):
1) Unit tests + integration test that asserts telemetry tags are emitted for each fallback path.
2) Canary on 1-2 low-traffic regions for 48 hours with metric gates: no p99 regression > 15%, no accuracy regression (if applicable) > 2%.
3) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 75% over 24 hours with manual pause gates.
4) Full release with post-release monitoring for 72 hours.

Operational ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Platform SRE team (oncall rotation: platform-sre)
- Escalation: Runtime reliability (pager: runtime-leads)
- Product/UX consult: Product Platform PM (Elena Rodriguez)

FAQ and examples:
Q: When should we prefer partial responses over model downgrades?
A: Prefer partial responses when the client can render partial content (e.g., streaming chat or progressive embeddings). If semantics must be preserved, prefer model downgrade only if it has been pre-validated.

Q: How do we measure user impact objectively?
A: Use a combination of latency percentiles, error surface area (fraction of failing calls), and downstream semantic quality metrics (self-bleu, automated evals tied to the prompt set).

Related artifacts and runbooks:
- See runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/service-registry-schema-migration-and-alerting-runbook-2026
- Telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/observability-contracts-and-dependency-slo-onboarding-handbook-2025

Appendix A: Example telemetry mapping (CSV-style lines):
metric_name,description,aggregation
degradation.count,number of degraded responses,sum
degradation.rate,ratio vs total,avg
degradation.latency.p99,p99 latency of degraded requests,p99

Appendix B: Short checklist for new service owners:
- [ ] Add "Degradation" row to dashboard
- [ ] Ensure telemetry tags are emitted for all fallback paths
- [ ] Add canary gate for any automated downgrade
- [ ] Document expected UX change for each strategy

If you have additions or want to propose a new strategy, open an RFC and tag platform-sre and runtime-leads. This page is the canonical decision catalog for degradation behavior; keep it updated after retrospectives and production incidents.
